nameStory: Canthocamptus sinuus gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'bent foot' (cantho-camptus) and 'winding' (sinuus), referring to its curved swimming legs and the sinuous way it moves through water. This tiny crustacean doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists and nature enthusiasts simply call it by its genus name, Canthocamptus. The 'bent foot' description becomes clear when you watch one swim - its legs curve and flex in a distinctive rowing motion.
description: Canthocamptus sinuus is a microscopic freshwater copepod - a tiny shrimp-like crustacean that's part of the zooplankton community in ponds and slow streams. These translucent creatures are incredibly small, measuring less than 1 millimeter long (about the width of a penny's thickness). They have an elongated, somewhat flattened body with a distinct head region and long antennae that they use for swimming and sensing their environment. Unlike their free-swimming copepod cousins, Canthocamptus species spend much of their time crawling along the bottom sediments and among aquatic plants.

idTips.label: Body shape and movement
idTips.description: Look for a tiny, translucent creature with a distinctly segmented body that moves in a characteristic jerky, stop-and-go pattern rather than smooth swimming

idTips.label: Size reference
idTips.description: Extremely small - you'll need a magnifying glass or microscope to see details, roughly the size of a large grain of salt

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two prominent, multi-segmented antennae extending from the front that are nearly as long as the body itself

idTips.label: Swimming legs
idTips.description: Multiple pairs of feathery, curved swimming legs (pleopods) that create a distinctive rowing motion when observed under magnification

idTips.label: Habitat preference
idTips.description: Found crawling along muddy or sandy bottom sediments rather than free-swimming in open water like many other copepods

habitat: Look for Canthocamptus sinuus in shallow freshwater environments throughout New England, particularly in the muddy or sandy sediments of pond edges, slow-moving streams, and marshy areas. They prefer areas with some organic matter and plant debris where they can find food and shelter. You'll often find them in the same habitats as other small aquatic invertebrates, typically in water less than a few feet deep with gentle or no current.

seasonality.spring: Active as water temperatures rise, with populations beginning to increase. Look for them in shallow areas that warm up first.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity and reproduction period. Most abundant during warm months when you're most likely to spot them with a magnifying glass.
seasonality.fall: Still active but populations may begin to decline. Continue looking in the same shallow water habitats.
seasonality.winter: Activity greatly reduced in frozen areas, but may remain active under ice in deeper sections that don't freeze solid.

funFact: Despite being smaller than most grains of sand, Canthocamptus copepods are incredibly important to freshwater ecosystems - a single pond can contain millions of them, and they can filter and clean more water than much larger aquatic animals by constantly feeding on bacteria, algae, and organic particles.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other microscopic copepods, but Canthocamptus can be distinguished by its bottom-dwelling behavior and less streamlined body shape compared to the torpedo-shaped free-swimming copepods like Cyclops. Remember: Canthocamptus crawls while Cyclops cruises.
contextualKnowledge: The observation count of only 2 in New England doesn't mean this species is rare - it likely reflects the specialized equipment and expertise needed to properly identify microscopic copepods. Many similar-looking species in this group require expert examination to distinguish, so citizen science reports are uncommon.
compareHints: Since no other Canthocamptus species appear in the regional dataset, compare with other harpacticoid copepods in the family Canthocamptidae by looking for the characteristic bottom-dwelling behavior and robust body shape. Canthocamptus species generally have a more cylindrical, less compressed body compared to other members of their family, and their swimming legs tend to be more developed for crawling than pure swimming.
